overview: Latvia restored full independence in 1991 after decades of occupation. The renewed parliamentary republic joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2014. Its recent history includes new public institutions, converted scientific equipment and communities keeping local traditions alive.

periods.title: Restoration and European integration
periods.summary: Independence returned and Latvia prepared for European Union membership.

periods.title: A member of the European Union
periods.summary: EU membership began in 2004; the euro replaced the lats in 2014.

items.text: On 18 January 2014, thousands of people formed a human chain to pass books from Latvia’s old National Library building to its new home. The ceremonial move made readers part of the opening celebrations. A book could cross the city with a remarkable number of helping hands.

The library’s People’s Bookshelf invited readers to donate a book with a personal note on its title page. Donated volumes were displayed in a glass wall rising through several floors. The collection preserves people’s attachments to books as well as the books themselves.

At Irbene, former Soviet military intelligence antennas gained a scientific future after Russian troops withdrew in 1994. Researchers established a radio astronomy centre using dishes 32 and 16 metres across. Equipment once associated with secrecy became part of international efforts to study the universe.

Irbene’s later telescope upgrades included extremely cold radio receivers to help measure faint signals. A research paper reports one part operating at 14 kelvin, close to absolute zero. From October 2015 the upgraded 32-metre telescope took part in joint international observing sessions.

MikroTik was registered in Latvia in 1996 and develops networking products including routers, switches and wireless systems. These devices help move information between computers. Latvia’s modern technical work therefore includes the ordinary-looking boxes that let other people’s computers talk to each other.

Riga’s Daugavgrīva wastewater plant began operating in 1991. Sewage passes through mechanical cleaning before biological treatment using activated sludge, and a laboratory checks the treated water. Flushing a toilet starts a journey that needs pipes, pumps and a great deal of organized work.

Daugavgrīva’s equipment was upgraded in 1999, including aeration, screens and grit traps. Further biological treatment improvements followed in 2014. A functioning modern city depends on repeated investment in this hidden infrastructure, even when its residents rarely think about what happens after the flush.

The Suiti community in western Latvia combines Catholic religious traditions with older local customs and modern life. Its cultural identity includes distinctive dress, food, celebrations and women’s drone singing, in which a sustained vocal sound accompanies the melody.

The Suiti Cultural Heritage Foundation, established in 2013, organizes informal learning for ages ranging from preschool children to seniors. Its work connects handicrafts, music, local speech and seasonal celebrations. Keeping a tradition alive involves opportunities to practise it together, rather than only storing it in an archive.

Latvia’s Song and Dance Celebration grows from rehearsals in local groups and community centres. Most participants are amateurs, guided by conductors and instructors. The large festival is the visible result of many smaller evenings spent practising with neighbours, friends and fellow singers.

In 1998 Latvia added a fundamental-rights chapter to its constitution. It includes protection for minority communities’ languages and cultural identities. These rights matter in schools, cultural associations and family life in a country whose residents have several linguistic and cultural backgrounds.

Latvian, article 112 of the constitution’s modern rights chapter: “Ikvienam ir tiesības uz izglītību.” Translation: “Everyone has the right to education.” The quotation follows the Saeima’s Latvian consolidated text. This chapter was added in 1998, long after the original 1922 constitution.

ending.text: Latvia continues as an independent republic. Its 1991 restoration renewed the state established in 1918; the map’s 1994 label marks later coverage. Membership in the European Union is a subsequent chapter in that continuing history.
